domain: Political Theory / International Law / Territorial Sovereignty
topic_summary: Analysis of competing legitimacy claims over the same territory between Israeli and Palestinian polities. The dispute centers on whether this is one contested kernel (territorial-legitimacy) read differently by two parties, or two entirely distinct kernels with no shared normative substrate. This is a deliberate coherence-boundary test.

key_entities: State of Israel (established 1948; claims sovereignty via UN partition, self-determination, and security necessity)
Palestinian Authority / PLO (claims sovereignty via indigenous presence, self-determination, and international law)
UN Security Council (international legal authority; Resolution 242, 338, etc.)
International Court of Justice (advisory opinions on wall, settlements)
Hamas (Gaza governing authority; rejects two-state framework)
Israeli settlement enterprise (territorial facts on ground; ~700,000 settlers in West Bank/East Jerusalem)
key_tensions: Self-determination claims: both invoke same principle, different temporal/demographic baselines
Security vs occupation: Israeli security necessity vs Palestinian territorial integrity
Historical continuity: ancient Jewish presence vs continuous Arab/Palestinian habitation
key_mechanisms: Settlement expansion: incremental territorial control via civilian population transfer
UN resolutions: international legal framework largely unenforced
key_absences: Enforcement mechanism for international law (resolutions exist, compliance does not)
Agreed historical baseline (1948, 1967, 1917, Biblical era all invoked)
Third-party adjudication with binding authority (ICJ advisory only)

omegas.description: Is territorial_legitimacy genuinely ONE kernel read differently, or two incommensurable kernels (Jewish self-determination vs Palestinian self-determination) with no shared substrate? The readings share the FORM of legitimacy claims but may not share normative grounding. If incommensurable, the dispute is not about interpretation but about which kernel exists.

International law enforceability is classified as rope (coordination) but functions as mountain (physical power asymmetry) in practice. Deferred axis may warrant reclassification if enforcement is structurally impossible rather than merely absent.
omegas.source: Deferred axis international_law_enforceability; Dark Matter Probe 3

omegas.description: Self-determination baseline selection appears arbitrary (why 1948 vs 1917 vs 1967?) but each baseline generates different victim/beneficiary sets. The choice of baseline IS the constraint, not a parameter of it. Possible tangled_rope misclassification.
omegas.source: Axis self_determination_baseline classification; F03 hasty generalization check

omegas.description: Partition reading may collapse into security_occupation reading if 'temporary partition for security' becomes 'permanent partition via occupation.' The two readings may not be structurally independent over time.
omegas.source: §3 independence testing; readings may merge under prolonged occupation

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: Territorial legitimacy: the shared commitment that legitimate sovereignty over territory requires a grounding claim (self-determination, historical presence, legal recognition, security necessity). Parties agree sovereignty requires justification but read the justification requirements differently.
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: International law (UN Charter, UNSC resolutions, ICJ opinions) claims interpretive authority but lacks enforcement mechanism. Competing authorities: Israeli domestic law, Palestinian national movement, regional powers, religious texts.

readings.commitment: Legitimacy via international legal partition and state recognition (UN Resolution 181, 1948 borders)
readings.authority_grounding: UN partition plan, international recognition, self-determination for both peoples
readings.expected_structural_delta: Both Israeli and Palestinian states legitimate within recognized borders; settlements beyond 1967 lines illegitimate; two-state solution structurally possible

readings.commitment: Legitimacy via security necessity and defensive territorial control (1967 borders plus strategic depth)
readings.authority_grounding: Self-defense under international law, existential threat narrative, strategic military requirements
readings.expected_structural_delta: Israeli control of West Bank/Golan legitimate as security buffer; Palestinian sovereignty conditional on demilitarization; settlements legitimate as security presence

readings.commitment: Legitimacy via continuous indigenous habitation and anti-colonial self-determination (1948 as Nakba, not partition)
readings.authority_grounding: Indigenous rights, anti-colonial international law, continuous habitation since pre-1948
readings.expected_structural_delta: Palestinian sovereignty over all of historic Palestine; Israeli state illegitimate as settler-colonial entity; right of return for 1948 refugees structurally central
